explanation: Windows Server 2025 machines connected to Azure Arc can be enabled for Hotpatch, which applies OS security updates without a restart in most months. Cluster-Aware Updating orchestrates rolling restarts for failover clusters, automatic VM guest patching applies to Azure VMs and WSUS deadlines still lead to restarts.

prompt: An administrator wants Azure Update Manager to check Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers for missing updates automatically every day without installing anything. What should be enabled?

options.text: A maintenance configuration with a daily recurrence
Automatic VM guest patching
A one-time update
Periodic assessment

explanation: Periodic assessment makes Update Manager scan machines for missing updates every 24 hours without installing them. A maintenance configuration schedules installations, automatic VM guest patching installs updates on Azure VMs and a one-time update installs updates immediately.

prompt: An administrator created an Azure Update Manager maintenance configuration that runs on the third Saturday of each month. New servers tagged PatchGroup=Wave2 must join this schedule automatically without editing it. What should be used?

options.text: A dynamic scope that filters on the PatchGroup=Wave2 tag
A static list of machines that is updated each week
A periodic assessment policy assignment
An Azure Automation webhook

explanation: Dynamic scopes evaluate criteria such as subscription, resource group, location, OS type and tags when the schedule runs, so newly tagged machines are included automatically. A static machine list must be edited, periodic assessment only scans for updates and a webhook starts runbooks rather than defining patch targets.

prompt: A team moving from the retired Azure Automation Update Management solution asks what Azure Update Manager requires for Arc-enabled servers. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It requires the Log Analytics agent and a linked Automation account
It requires a Log Analytics workspace to store assessment results before any patches can be installed
It works natively on Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers without depending on Log Analytics or Azure Automation
It requires Windows Server Update Services on each server as the update source

explanation: Azure Update Manager is built into Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers and has no dependency on Log Analytics or Azure Automation. The Log Analytics agent, workspace and Automation account dependencies belonged to the older Update Management solution. WSUS can be an update source but isn't required.

prompt: A critical out-of-band security update must be installed today on 25 Arc-enabled servers, outside the normal monthly maintenance window. What should the administrator do in Azure Update Manager?

options.text: Change the periodic assessment to run every hour
Run a one-time update on the selected machines that includes the update
Wait for the next run of the maintenance configuration
Assign a machine configuration policy to the servers

explanation: A one-time update installs selected updates immediately on chosen machines, outside any schedule. Assessment only detects missing updates, waiting for the maintenance window misses the deadline and machine configuration doesn't install Windows updates.

prompt: An Azure Automation runbook must clean up files on on-premises servers that can't accept inbound connections from Azure. Where should the runbook run?

options.text: In an Azure sandbox in the same region as the Automation account
In an Azure Container Instance that the runbook starts
In an Azure Function that the runbook calls
On a Hybrid Runbook Worker on an Arc-enabled on-premises server

explanation: A Hybrid Runbook Worker runs jobs locally on the machine and communicates outbound with Azure, and the extension-based worker is supported on Arc-enabled servers. Azure sandboxes, container instances and Functions run in Azure and can't reach the on-premises servers without additional networking.

prompt: A runbook must stop Azure VMs that have a specific tag. It must authenticate to Azure without storing any credentials or certificates. What should be used?

options.text: The Automation account's managed identity with Connect-AzAccount -Identity
A Run As account created in the Automation account
A credential asset that contains a Global Administrator's password
A shared access signature for the subscription

explanation: A managed identity on the Automation account, granted a suitable Azure role, lets the runbook sign in with Connect-AzAccount -Identity without stored secrets. Run As accounts have been retired, a credential asset stores a password for an over-privileged account and shared access signatures grant access to storage, not to a subscription.

prompt: A third-party monitoring system must start an Azure Automation runbook by sending an HTTP POST request when it detects a failed service. What should the administrator create?

options.text: A schedule linked to the runbook
A Hybrid Runbook Worker group
A webhook for the runbook
A variable asset in the Automation account

explanation: A webhook provides a unique URL that starts the runbook when it receives an HTTP POST and can pass data to it. Schedules start runbooks at set times, Hybrid Runbook Worker groups define where jobs run and variable assets store values used by runbooks.

prompt: A PowerShell runbook must run every weekday at 06:00 to produce a report, without depending on any system outside Azure Automation. What should be configured?

options.text: A webhook called by a scheduled task on an on-premises server
A recurring schedule in the Automation account linked to the runbook
A data collection rule with a 24-hour collection frequency
A maintenance configuration in Azure Update Manager

explanation: Azure Automation schedules can recur weekly on chosen days and be linked to runbooks. A webhook called by an on-premises scheduled task depends on an outside system. Data collection rules gather monitoring data, and maintenance configurations schedule updates rather than runbooks.

prompt: Administrators who connect to VMs on a Windows Server 2025 Hyper-V host by using Virtual Machine Connection can't copy and paste files or redirect USB devices, and the Enhanced session option isn't offered. What should the administrator do on the host?

options.text: Enable the Guest Service Interface integration service on each VM
Run Set-VMHost -EnableEnhancedSessionMode $true
Enable nested virtualization for each VM with Set-VMProcessor
Add the administrators to the Hyper-V Administrators group

explanation: Enhanced session mode is off by default on Windows Server Hyper-V hosts and is turned on with Set-VMHost -EnableEnhancedSessionMode $true or in Hyper-V Settings; it uses RDP over VMBus to provide clipboard, drive and USB redirection. The Guest Service Interface supports Copy-VMFile rather than VMConnect redirection. Nested virtualization and Hyper-V Administrators membership don't enable enhanced sessions.

prompt: A Windows Server 2025 VM was given an incorrect IP configuration and has no network connectivity. An administrator signed in to the Hyper-V host must run PowerShell commands inside the VM to fix it. What should the administrator use?

options.text: Enter-PSSession -ComputerName with the VM's host name
Enter-PSSession -HostName with an SSH key
Invoke-Command -ComputerName with CredSSP authentication
Enter-PSSession -VMName with credentials for the guest

explanation: PowerShell Direct, used with -VMName or -VMId, connects from the Hyper-V host to a Windows guest over VMBus and needs only guest credentials, not network connectivity. -ComputerName, -HostName and CredSSP-based connections all travel over the network, which isn't working.

prompt: An administrator wants to run the Hyper-V role inside a VM named LAB1 for a test environment. Which command must be run on the host while LAB1 is turned off?

options.text: Set-VMProcessor -VMName LAB1 -ExposeVirtualizationExtensions $true
Set-VM -VMName LAB1 -CheckpointType ProductionOnly
Set-VMMemory -VMName LAB1 -DynamicMemoryEnabled $true
Enable-VMIntegrationService -VMName LAB1 -Name 'Guest Service Interface'

explanation: Nested virtualization requires exposing the processor's virtualization extensions to the VM with Set-VMProcessor -ExposeVirtualizationExtensions $true while the VM is off. The checkpoint type, dynamic memory and the Guest Service Interface don't let a hypervisor run inside the guest.

prompt: Nested virtualization is enabled on VM LAB1. Nested VMs inside LAB1 are connected to an external virtual switch in LAB1 but can't reach the physical network. Which change on the outer host lets the nested VMs' traffic pass through LAB1's network adapter?

options.text: Enable DHCP guard on LAB1's network adapter
Enable router guard on LAB1's network adapter
Enable MAC address spoofing on LAB1's network adapter
Set a maximum bandwidth on LAB1's network adapter

explanation: Frames from nested VMs carry their own MAC addresses, so the outer VM's adapter needs MAC address spoofing (Set-VMNetworkAdapter -MacAddressSpoofing On), or the nested VMs can use NAT instead. DHCP guard and router guard drop DHCP server and router advertisement messages, and a bandwidth limit doesn't affect MAC filtering.

prompt: A VM that uses dynamic memory needs 4 GB of RAM while its application services start but only about 1.5 GB afterward. The host is short of memory. How should dynamic memory be configured?

options.text: Startup RAM 1.5 GB, minimum RAM 1.5 GB, maximum RAM 4 GB
Startup RAM 4 GB, minimum RAM 1.5 GB, maximum RAM 4 GB or more
Static memory of 4 GB with the default memory weight
Startup RAM 4 GB, minimum RAM 4 GB, memory buffer of 0 percent

explanation: Startup RAM is what the VM gets when it boots, and the minimum RAM lets Hyper-V reclaim memory afterward, so 4 GB at startup with a 1.5 GB minimum fits this workload. A 1.5 GB startup value may not be enough to start the services. Static memory or a 4 GB minimum keeps 4 GB allocated permanently, which wastes memory on a constrained host.

prompt: Several VMs with dynamic memory compete for memory on a busy host. The SQL Server VM must be given memory ahead of the test VMs when there isn't enough for all of them. Which setting should be raised on the SQL Server VM?

options.text: Memory buffer
Startup RAM
NUMA spanning
Memory weight

explanation: Memory weight sets the priority Hyper-V uses to decide which VMs get memory when demand exceeds what's available. The memory buffer is extra memory reserved above current demand, startup RAM affects only boot and NUMA spanning controls whether VMs can use memory across NUMA nodes.

prompt: An administrator runs Copy-VMFile to copy an installer from the Hyper-V host into a running VM, and the command fails. Which integration service must be enabled for the VM?

options.text: Guest Service Interface
Data Exchange
Heartbeat
Time Synchronization

explanation: Copy-VMFile depends on the Guest Service Interface integration service, which is disabled by default and can be turned on with Enable-VMIntegrationService. Data Exchange shares key-value pairs, Heartbeat reports whether the guest is responding and Time Synchronization keeps the guest clock aligned with the host.

prompt: An administrator must give a VM exclusive, direct access to a physical NVMe device by using Discrete Device Assignment (DDA). Which approach is correct?

options.text: Run Add-VMGpuPartitionAdapter for the VM, then run Dismount-VMHostAssignableDevice on the host
Run Set-VMHost -EnableEnhancedSessionMode $true, then run Add-VMAssignableDevice for the VM
Set the VM's stop action to TurnOff, dismount the device from the host, then run Add-VMAssignableDevice
Enable SR-IOV on the external virtual switch, then attach the device to the VM with Add-VMNetworkAdapter

explanation: For DDA, the VM's automatic stop action must be TurnOff, the device is disabled and dismounted from the host with Dismount-VMHostAssignableDevice and then assigned with Add-VMAssignableDevice. Add-VMGpuPartitionAdapter is for GPU partitioning, enhanced session mode is unrelated and SR-IOV with Add-VMNetworkAdapter configures virtual network adapters rather than passing through a device.

prompt: A company wants to run 12 VDI virtual machines on one Windows Server 2025 Hyper-V host that has a single supported GPU, with each VM receiving a dedicated, hardware-isolated share of the GPU. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: Discrete Device Assignment of the GPU to each of the VMs
GPU partitioning, with Add-VMGpuPartitionAdapter run for each VM
RemoteFX vGPU adapters for each of the VMs
Enhanced session mode with GPU redirection for each VM

explanation: GPU partitioning uses SR-IOV to give each VM a dedicated fraction of a supported GPU, and partitions are added to VMs with Add-VMGpuPartitionAdapter. DDA dedicates an entire GPU to one VM, and a GPU can't be assigned with DDA and partitioning at the same time. RemoteFX vGPU has been removed from Hyper-V, and enhanced session mode doesn't share a GPU.

prompt: Checkpoints of the application server VM APP1 must always be application-consistent. If the guest can't create a VSS-based checkpoint, no checkpoint should be taken. Which command should the administrator run?

options.text: Set-VM -Name APP1 -CheckpointType Standard
Set-VM -Name APP1 -CheckpointType Production
Set-VM -Name APP1 -CheckpointType Disabled
Set-VM -Name APP1 -CheckpointType ProductionOnly

explanation: ProductionOnly creates production checkpoints, which use VSS in Windows guests, and fails instead of falling back to a standard checkpoint. Production falls back to a standard checkpoint when a production checkpoint can't be created, Standard captures memory and device state without VSS and Disabled prevents checkpoints altogether.

prompt: A VM's folder contains several large .avhdx files from checkpoints that are no longer needed, and the volume is running out of space. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Remove the checkpoints with Remove-VMCheckpoint so the differencing disks merge
Delete the .avhdx files in File Explorer while the VM runs so the parent disk is used
Run Optimize-VHD on each .avhdx file to compact it in place
Convert each .avhdx file to a fixed disk with Convert-VHD

explanation: Deleting checkpoints through Hyper-V Manager or Remove-VMCheckpoint merges each .avhdx differencing disk into its parent and removes the files safely. Deleting .avhdx files manually breaks the disk chain and can lose data. Optimize-VHD compacts dynamic disks but keeps the checkpoint chain, and fixed disks would use more space.

prompt: A node in a Hyper-V failover cluster needs a firmware update that requires a restart. The node's highly available VMs must keep running during the maintenance. What should the administrator do first?

options.text: Shut down the VMs on the node, then restart the node and start the VMs again
Run Stop-ClusterNode on the node
Drain the node's roles, for example with Suspend-ClusterNode -Drain
Enable Hyper-V Replica for every VM on the node

explanation: Pausing and draining a node live-migrates its clustered VMs to other nodes before maintenance, so they keep running. Shutting down the VMs causes downtime, and Stop-ClusterNode stops the cluster service without first live-migrating the roles. Hyper-V Replica provides disaster recovery and doesn't move running VMs.

prompt: A running Generation 2 VM has a 200 GB VHDX data disk attached to its SCSI controller, and the disk must grow to 400 GB without downtime. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Shut down the VM, run Convert-VHD to a fixed disk, then extend the partition
Run Resize-VHD while the VM runs, then extend the volume in the guest
Add a differencing disk to the VHDX and merge it into the parent disk
Run Optimize-VHD -Mode Full on the VHDX while the VM runs

explanation: A VHDX attached to a SCSI controller can be expanded while the VM runs with Resize-VHD or the Edit Disk wizard, after which the volume is extended inside the guest. Shutting the VM down causes downtime, and converting the disk type doesn't enlarge it. Differencing disks record changes rather than adding capacity, and Optimize-VHD reclaims unused space in dynamic disks.

prompt: A developer's VM on a shared Hyper-V host was accidentally configured as a DHCP server and is handing out addresses to other VMs on the same virtual switch. How can the administrator stop the VM from answering DHCP requests without changing the guest?

options.text: Enable router guard on the VM's network adapter
Enable MAC address spoofing on the VM's network adapter
Move the VM to an internal virtual switch
Enable DHCP guard on the VM's network adapter

explanation: DHCP guard drops DHCP server messages from a VM that isn't authorized to act as a DHCP server. Router guard drops router advertisement and redirect messages, and MAC address spoofing allows a VM to send frames from other MAC addresses. On an internal switch the VM could still answer DHCP requests from the host and other VMs on that switch.

prompt: A new Windows Server 2025 Hyper-V host has two 25 GbE RDMA-capable adapters. The administrator wants fault tolerance and to share both adapters between VM traffic and host traffic on one virtual switch. What should be configured?

options.text: A virtual switch created with New-VMSwitch -EnableEmbeddedTeaming $true and both adapters
An LBFO team created with New-NetLbfoTeam and an external virtual switch bound to it
Two external virtual switches, each bound to one of the adapters
An internal virtual switch with NIC teaming configured inside each VM

explanation: Switch Embedded Teaming (SET) builds teaming into the Hyper-V virtual switch, supports RDMA and is the recommended teaming option for Hyper-V hosts. LBFO teams are deprecated for use with the Hyper-V switch and are blocked by default starting with Windows Server 2022. Separate switches don't give host-level failover, and an internal switch doesn't reach the physical network.

prompt: An isolated lab requires VMs that can communicate with each other and with the Hyper-V host, but not with the physical network. Which type of virtual switch should be created?

options.text: External
Private
Internal
External with management OS sharing turned off

explanation: An internal switch connects VMs to each other and to the host's management OS without access to the physical network. A private switch connects only the VMs and excludes the host. An external switch bridges to a physical adapter, and turning off management OS sharing removes only the host's access while VMs still reach the physical network.

prompt: An administrator wants to replicate VMs from a standalone Hyper-V server to a Hyper-V failover cluster at a disaster recovery site by using Hyper-V Replica. What must be configured on the cluster?

options.text: A Scale-Out File Server role
The Hyper-V Replica Broker role
Storage Replica between the cluster nodes
Cluster-Aware Updating

explanation: A failover cluster that acts as a Replica server needs the Hyper-V Replica Broker role, which provides a client access point and tracks which node owns each replica VM. A Scale-Out File Server provides storage, Storage Replica replicates volumes rather than individual VMs and Cluster-Aware Updating patches cluster nodes.

prompt: An organization must show each quarter that VMs replicated with Hyper-V Replica can start at the recovery site, without interrupting replication or affecting the production VMs. Which action should the administrator perform on the replica VMs?

options.text: Planned failover
Failover
Reverse replication
Test failover

explanation: Test failover creates a temporary test VM from a recovery point on the Replica server while replication continues and the primary keeps running. A planned failover shuts down the primary VM, a failover brings the replica online as the production copy and reverse replication changes the direction of replication.

prompt: A team deploys a Windows Server VM in Azure that hosts a rarely used archive application for internal testing. They want the lowest storage cost and accept lower performance. Which managed disk type should they use for the data disk?

options.text: Premium SSD v2
Ultra Disk
Standard HDD
Premium SSD

explanation: Standard HDD has the lowest cost and suits dev/test, backup and infrequently accessed workloads. Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk provide higher performance at a higher price for production and latency-sensitive workloads.

prompt: An administrator is configuring a SQL Server VM in Azure with separate Premium SSD disks for data files and transaction log files. Which two host caching settings follow Microsoft's recommendations?

options.text: ReadOnly for the data file disks
ReadWrite for the data file disks
None for the transaction log disks
ReadWrite for the transaction log disks
ReadOnly for the transaction log disks

explanation: Microsoft recommends ReadOnly host caching for data file disks, which benefit from cached reads, and None for transaction log disks, because the log is written sequentially and gains nothing from caching. ReadWrite caching on either disk risks the integrity of SQL Server files, and ReadOnly caching on log disks provides no benefit for a write-heavy log.

prompt: An administrator saved a nightly export to drive D: of a Windows Server VM in Azure. After the VM was stopped (deallocated) and started again, the export was gone. What is the cause?

options.text: Drive D: is a Standard HDD disk that Azure Backup resets after each backup
The disk encryption set rotated its key and cleared the data
The Windows page file overwrote the export during startup
Drive D: is the temporary disk, which isn't persisted across deallocation

explanation: On VM sizes with a local temporary disk, it usually appears as D: and is intended for temporary data such as the page file; its contents can be lost when the VM is deallocated, redeployed or moved during maintenance. Azure Backup and key rotation don't erase data, and the page file doesn't overwrite other files on the volume.

prompt: Compliance requires that the managed disks of Azure VMs be encrypted at rest with keys that the company controls in Azure Key Vault. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: Nothing, because platform-managed keys already meet this requirement
A disk encryption set that uses a Key Vault key, applied to the disks
BitLocker in each guest with the recovery key saved on the OS disk
Storage Service Encryption on the storage account that holds the disks

explanation: Managed disks are always encrypted at rest; to use customer-managed keys, the administrator creates a disk encryption set that references a Key Vault key and associates it with the disks. Platform-managed keys are controlled by Microsoft. A recovery key stored on the same disk defeats the purpose, and managed disks don't live in a customer storage account whose settings could be changed.

prompt: An administrator tries to resize a running Azure VM to a larger size, but the desired size isn't listed as available for the VM. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Stop (deallocate) the VM, and then select the new size
Delete the VM and redeploy it from a marketplace image
Add the VM to an availability set before resizing
Increase the size of the VM's OS disk first

explanation: If the target size isn't available on the hardware cluster that hosts the running VM, deallocating it lets Azure place it on hardware that supports the new size. Redeploying from an image is unnecessary, an existing VM can't be added to an availability set and disk size doesn't determine which VM sizes are offered.

prompt: A web tier runs on identical Windows Server VMs. Demand spikes unpredictably, and the company wants Azure to add VMs when average CPU exceeds 70 percent and remove them when demand falls. What should be used?

options.text: An availability set with three fault domains
Azure Update Manager with a dynamic scope
A virtual machine scale set with an autoscale rule based on CPU
A larger VM size selected through vertical resizing

explanation: Virtual machine scale sets add and remove instances automatically according to autoscale rules such as average CPU percentage. Availability sets spread VMs across fault and update domains but don't scale, Update Manager patches machines and vertical resizing changes one VM's size, usually with a restart.

prompt: Two domain controller VMs are deployed in an Azure region that doesn't offer availability zones. They must not fail together because of a rack failure or planned host maintenance. What should be used?

options.text: A proximity placement group
An availability set
A virtual machine scale set with one instance
Azure Site Recovery replication within the same region

explanation: An availability set places VMs in different fault domains (racks) and update domains, so a hardware failure or planned maintenance doesn't affect both at once. A proximity placement group keeps VMs physically close, which increases shared risk, a single-instance scale set has no redundancy and Site Recovery replicates for disaster recovery rather than spreading running VMs.

prompt: An application's two Windows Server VMs must stay available even if an entire Azure datacenter in the region fails. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Place both VMs in the same availability set
Place both VMs in one proximity placement group
Use Premium SSD disks for both VMs
Deploy the VMs into different availability zones

explanation: Availability zones are physically separate datacenters in a region, so VMs in different zones survive the loss of one datacenter. An availability set protects against rack and maintenance failures inside one datacenter, a proximity placement group keeps VMs close together and the disk type doesn't affect datacenter resiliency.

prompt: An administrator wants an existing, running Azure VM to become part of an availability set that was created later. What must be done?

options.text: Recreate the VM in the availability set, reusing its existing disks
Stop the VM and change its availability set property in the portal
Move the VM into the availability set's resource group
Resize the VM to a size that the availability set supports, then restart it

explanation: A VM's availability set is chosen when the VM is created and can't be changed afterward, so the VM must be recreated in the set, typically by deleting it while keeping its disks and creating a new VM from them. Stopping, moving or resizing the VM doesn't place it in an availability set.

prompt: An administrator is creating an availability set in a region that supports three fault domains. Which statement about availability sets is correct?

options.text: Up to 20 fault domains and 3 update domains can be configured
Update domains protect against rack power failures, and fault domains group VMs for planned maintenance
Up to 3 fault domains and 20 update domains can be configured, with 5 update domains by default
Each VM in the set is automatically placed in a different availability zone

explanation: Availability sets support up to three fault domains, depending on the region, and up to 20 update domains, with five update domains by default. Fault domains share power and network hardware and update domains group VMs for planned maintenance, not the reverse, and availability sets don't place VMs in availability zones.

prompt: An administrator wants to use just-in-time VM access so that RDP stays closed on Azure VMs until someone requests it. What is required?

options.text: Microsoft Defender for Servers Plan 1
Microsoft Defender for Servers Plan 2
Azure Bastion Premium SKU
Azure Update Manager

explanation: Just-in-time VM access is a Defender for Servers Plan 2 feature in Microsoft Defender for Cloud. Plan 1 focuses on the Defender for Endpoint integration and doesn't include JIT. Azure Bastion provides RDP and SSH without exposed ports but isn't what JIT requires, and Update Manager handles patching.

prompt: Just-in-time VM access is enabled for a VM. A user requests RDP access for two hours from their current IP address. How does Defender for Cloud grant the access?

options.text: It assigns the user the Virtual Machine Administrator Login role for two hours
It deploys an Azure Bastion host for the duration of the request
It turns on Network Level Authentication on the VM for two hours
It temporarily allows port 3389 from the user's IP in the NSG or Azure Firewall

explanation: JIT keeps the management port denied in the network security group, and Azure Firewall if used, and adds a temporary allow rule for the requesting IP address and the approved duration. It doesn't change Azure role assignments, deploy Bastion or toggle Network Level Authentication.

prompt: An administrator is deploying an Azure Bastion host with the Standard SKU. What must exist in the virtual network?

options.text: A subnet named AzureBastionSubnet with a prefix of /26 or larger
A subnet named GatewaySubnet with a prefix of /27 or larger
A subnet named BastionSubnet with a prefix of /29
A subnet delegated to Microsoft.Network/dnsResolvers

explanation: Dedicated Bastion deployments (Basic, Standard and Premium) require a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet that is /26 or larger. GatewaySubnet is used by VPN and ExpressRoute gateways, Bastion doesn't use a subnet named BastionSubnet and subnets delegated to Microsoft.Network/dnsResolvers host DNS Private Resolver endpoints.

prompt: Administrators want to connect to Azure VMs through Azure Bastion by using the native Windows Remote Desktop client launched from the Azure CLI, including file upload and download. Which is the lowest Bastion SKU that supports this?

options.text: Developer
Basic
Standard
Premium

explanation: Native client connections and file transfer require the Standard SKU or higher. Developer and Basic support only portal-based connections, and Premium also supports native clients but adds session recording and private-only deployment, so it isn't the lowest SKU.

prompt: Auditors require that every RDP and SSH session to Azure VMs through Azure Bastion be recorded. Which Bastion configuration meets this requirement?

options.text: Standard SKU with host scaling enabled
Basic SKU with two instances
Developer SKU in a supported region
Premium SKU

explanation: Session recording is available only with the Premium SKU. Standard adds native client support and host scaling without recording, Basic has a fixed two-instance capacity without advanced features and Developer is a free shared offering for one VM connection at a time.

prompt: An NSG on a VM's subnet has rule 100, which denies TCP 3389 from any source, and rule 200, which allows TCP 3389 from the admin network 10.50.0.0/24. Administrators can't connect with RDP. What should be done?

options.text: Change the priority of rule 200 to 4096
Give the allow rule a lower priority number than the deny rule, such as 90
Add the same allow rule to the NSG on the VM's network interface with priority 300
Remove the default AllowVnetInBound rule from the NSG

explanation: NSG rules are evaluated in priority order, lowest number first, and processing stops at the first match, so the deny rule at 100 wins until the allow rule has a lower number. Priority 4096 would be evaluated even later. An allow rule on the NIC doesn't help while the subnet NSG still denies the traffic, and default rules can't be removed.

prompt: An administrator must add a second network interface to an existing Azure VM so that it can connect to a separate backend subnet. What is required?

options.text: The VM must be deallocated, and its size must allow a second NIC
The VM must be running so that Windows can detect the new adapter
The second NIC must be in a different virtual network from the first NIC
A public IP address must be assigned to the second NIC

explanation: NICs can be added to or removed from a VM only while it's deallocated, and each VM size supports a maximum number of NICs. All of a VM's NICs must be in the same virtual network, though they can use different subnets, and a public IP address isn't required.

prompt: An administrator assigns a Standard SKU public IP address to an Azure VM that has no network security group. Inbound RDP to the public IP address still fails. Why?

options.text: Standard SKU public IP addresses support only outbound traffic
RDP connections require a Basic SKU public IP address
Standard SKU public IPs block inbound traffic unless an NSG allows it
The VM must also be deployed in an availability zone

explanation: Standard SKU public IP addresses are secure by default and closed to inbound traffic until a network security group explicitly allows it. They do accept inbound connections once allowed, RDP doesn't need a Basic SKU address and availability zones aren't required for inbound access.

prompt: DNS records in the corp.contoso.com zone must be updated dynamically only by authenticated domain members, so that unauthorized computers can't register or overwrite records. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: Convert the zone to a standard primary zone and allow nonsecure and secure updates
Store the zone in Active Directory and set dynamic updates to Secure only
Allow zone transfers only to the servers listed on the Name Servers tab
Create a GlobalNames zone and disable dynamic updates on it

explanation: Secure only dynamic updates are available only for Active Directory-integrated zones and require clients to authenticate before registering records. Nonsecure updates let any client register records, zone transfer restrictions control which servers receive copies of the zone and a GlobalNames zone provides single-label name resolution.

prompt: An AD-integrated zone named apps.contoso.com is stored in the domain partition of corp.contoso.com. DNS servers on domain controllers in a child domain of the same forest must also host the zone, without creating any additional directory partitions. Which replication scope should be selected?

options.text: To all domain controllers in this domain (for Windows 2000 compatibility)
To all DNS servers running on domain controllers in this domain
To all domain controllers in the scope of a custom directory partition
To all DNS servers running on domain controllers in this forest

explanation: The forest scope stores the zone in the ForestDnsZones partition, which replicates to every domain controller running DNS in the forest. Both domain scopes keep the zone within corp.contoso.com, and the custom partition scope would require creating and enlisting a new application partition.

prompt: Every DNS server on a domain controller in the forest must forward queries for fabrikam.com to 172.16.5.10, and the setting must replicate automatically to new DCs. Which command should the administrator run on one DC?

options.text: Add-DnsServerConditionalForwarderZone -Name fabrikam.com -MasterServers 172.16.5.10 -ReplicationScope Forest
Add-DnsServerForwarder -IPAddress 172.16.5.10
Add-DnsServerStubZone -Name fabrikam.com -MasterServers 172.16.5.10 -ZoneFile fabrikam.com.dns
Set-DnsServerForwarder -IPAddress 172.16.5.10 -UseRootHint $false

explanation: A conditional forwarder stored in Active Directory with -ReplicationScope Forest replicates to all DNS servers on DCs in the forest and forwards only fabrikam.com queries. Add-DnsServerForwarder and Set-DnsServerForwarder configure server-level forwarders for all unresolved queries, only on the server where they run. A file-backed stub zone isn't replicated through Active Directory.

prompt: Contoso resolves names in a partner's zone by sending queries to the partner's DNS servers. The partner often adds and retires authoritative DNS servers, although its primary server's address stays the same, and Contoso's settings keep going stale. Which solution keeps the list of the partner's authoritative servers current automatically?

options.text: A conditional forwarder for the partner zone
A secondary zone of the partner zone
A stub zone for the partner zone
A server-level forwarder to the partner's DNS servers

explanation: A stub zone holds the partner zone's SOA, NS and glue A records and refreshes them from its master server, so it learns about added and removed authoritative servers. Conditional and server-level forwarders use fixed IP lists that must be edited manually. A secondary zone copies the entire zone, which requires the partner to allow zone transfers and exposes more data than needed.

prompt: Internal DNS servers resolve internet names by using root hints. Security policy now requires that all external queries go through the ISP's filtered DNS servers. What should the administrator configure on the internal DNS servers?

options.text: A conditional forwarder for the com domain that points to the ISP's servers
Forwarders to the ISP's DNS servers, with root hint fallback disabled
Secondary zones for each internet domain that users visit
A GlobalNames zone that contains the ISP's DNS servers

explanation: Server-level forwarders send every query the server can't answer to the listed servers, and disabling root hint fallback (Set-DnsServerForwarder -UseRootHint $false) ensures queries never bypass them. A conditional forwarder for com would miss every other top-level domain, secondary zones for internet domains are impractical and need zone transfers and a GlobalNames zone serves single-label names.

prompt: Security tools need to resolve the IP addresses of servers in 10.40.0.0/16 back to host names, but reverse lookups fail. What should the administrator create?

options.text: A CNAME record for each server in the forward lookup zone
A conditional forwarder for in-addr.arpa
An SRV record for each server in the forward lookup zone
A 40.10.in-addr.arpa reverse lookup zone with PTR records

explanation: Reverse lookups query PTR records in an in-addr.arpa zone, so the 40.10.in-addr.arpa zone must exist with PTR records, which clients and DHCP can register dynamically. CNAME and SRV records belong in forward zones and map names to names or services. A conditional forwarder would send the queries elsewhere instead of answering them.

prompt: The research team runs its own DNS servers and wants to manage every record under research.contoso.com, while the corporate DNS team keeps managing contoso.com. What should be configured in the contoso.com zone?

options.text: A delegation for research.contoso.com to the research DNS servers
A secondary zone for research.contoso.com on the corporate DNS servers
A conditional forwarder for contoso.com on the research DNS servers
A CNAME record named research that points to the research DNS server

explanation: A delegation adds NS and glue records for research.contoso.com in the parent zone, so resolvers are referred to the research team's authoritative servers. A secondary zone is a read-only copy that wouldn't give the research team control. A conditional forwarder on the research servers doesn't affect how others find the subdomain, and a CNAME doesn't delegate a namespace.

prompt: An AD-integrated zone contains thousands of stale A records from decommissioned computers that registered dynamically. The administrator wants such records removed automatically. What should be configured?

options.text: Secure only dynamic updates on the zone
A shorter default TTL in the zone's SOA record
Aging on the zone and scavenging on at least one DNS server
Zone transfers restricted to the zone's name servers

explanation: Aging and scavenging deletes dynamically registered records whose timestamps haven't been refreshed within the no-refresh and refresh intervals; aging is enabled on the zone and scavenging on a DNS server. Secure updates control who can register records, the TTL controls caching by resolvers and transfer restrictions don't delete records.

prompt: The Azure Private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net is linked to a hub VNet that contains an Azure DNS Private Resolver. On-premises clients connected through a VPN must resolve private endpoint names in that zone. What should be configured on the on-premises DNS servers?

options.text: A conditional forwarder for blob.core.windows.net to 168.63.129.16
A conditional forwarder for blob.core.windows.net to the inbound endpoint IP
A secondary zone of privatelink.blob.core.windows.net transferred from Azure
A server-level forwarder to the IP address of the resolver's outbound endpoint

explanation: On-premises DNS servers resolve Azure private zones by conditionally forwarding the namespace to the Private Resolver's inbound endpoint. 168.63.129.16 is reachable only from inside Azure, Azure Private DNS zones don't support zone transfers to secondary servers and an outbound endpoint sends queries from Azure to other DNS servers rather than receiving them.

prompt: Azure VMs that use Azure-provided DNS must resolve names in the on-premises zone corp.contoso.com. An Azure DNS Private Resolver is deployed in the hub VNet. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: An inbound endpoint and a conditional forwarder on the on-premises DNS servers
A Private DNS zone named corp.contoso.com linked to the VNets
A custom DNS setting on each VNet that points to 168.63.129.16
An outbound endpoint and a forwarding ruleset linked to the VNets

explanation: An outbound endpoint with a DNS forwarding ruleset sends queries for corp.contoso.com to the on-premises DNS servers, and linking the ruleset to the VNets applies it without changing VM DNS settings. An inbound endpoint handles queries arriving from on-premises. A Private DNS zone with the same name would contain none of the on-premises records, and 168.63.129.16 is already the Azure-provided resolver.

prompt: Azure VMs use domain controllers running DNS in the same VNet as their DNS servers. The VMs must resolve names in an Azure Private DNS zone that is linked to that VNet. What should be configured on the DC DNS servers?

options.text: A conditional forwarder for the private zone's namespace to 168.63.129.16
A secondary zone of the Azure Private DNS zone
A delegation in the AD-integrated zone to the Azure DNS name servers
Root hints that include 168.63.129.16

explanation: 168.63.129.16 is the Azure-provided DNS virtual IP that answers for Private DNS zones linked to the VNet, so DNS servers in that VNet can forward the zone's namespace to it. Azure Private DNS zones don't support zone transfers, they aren't delegated from public name servers and root hints are used for iterative resolution from the root rather than forwarding.

prompt: An administrator created client subnets with Add-DnsServerClientSubnet and zone scopes with Add-DnsServerZoneScope so that clients in each office receive the address of their local web server. Which cmdlet creates the rule that sends each subnet's queries to the matching zone scope?

options.text: Add-DnsServerResourceRecord
Add-DnsServerZoneTransferPolicy
Add-DnsServerQueryResolutionPolicy
Add-DnsServerRecursionScope

explanation: Add-DnsServerQueryResolutionPolicy creates a policy that matches criteria such as the client subnet and answers from a specified zone scope. Add-DnsServerResourceRecord with -ZoneScope adds records to each scope but doesn't route queries, zone transfer policies control zone transfers and recursion scopes control recursion behavior.

prompt: A company wants one Windows DNS server to give internal clients the private IP address of www.contoso.com and give internet clients the public IP address, without maintaining two separate zones on different servers. What should be implemented?

options.text: A stub zone for contoso.com
DNS policies with zone scopes for internal and external clients
A GlobalNames zone that contains both of the www records
DNS round robin with both A records added to the contoso.com zone

explanation: DNS policies can answer from different zone scopes according to criteria such as the server interface or the client subnet, providing split-brain resolution from a single zone. A stub zone only lists authoritative servers, a GlobalNames zone serves single-label names and round robin returns both addresses to everyone in rotation.

prompt: A DNS server is flooded with queries from the malicious subnet 198.51.100.0/24. The administrator wants the server to drop queries from that subnet without affecting other clients. What should be configured?

options.text: A zone transfer policy that denies the subnet
A conditional forwarder that sends the subnet's queries to 127.0.0.1
Removal of the root hints from the server
A client subnet and a query resolution policy with the Ignore action for it

explanation: A query resolution policy can match a client subnet and use the Ignore action to drop its queries, or Deny to refuse them, while other clients are unaffected. A zone transfer policy applies only to zone transfer requests, a conditional forwarder matches a domain name rather than a client subnet and removing root hints breaks recursion for everyone.

prompt: An administrator signs the contoso.com zone with DNSSEC. Which key signs the zone's DNSKEY record set and serves as the basis of the trust anchor for validating resolvers?

options.text: The key signing key (KSK)
The zone signing key (ZSK)
The NSEC3 salt
The TSIG shared secret

explanation: The key signing key signs the DNSKEY record set, and its public key, or a DS record derived from it, is what validating resolvers use as a trust anchor. The zone signing key signs the zone's other record sets, the NSEC3 salt is used when hashing names for authenticated denial of existence and TSIG secrets authenticate DNS messages such as updates rather than signing zone data.

prompt: After signing an AD-integrated zone with DNSSEC, the administrator wants the other DNS servers on domain controllers in the forest to validate responses for that zone. What should be done?

options.text: Create a stub zone for the signed zone on each DNS server
Allow zone transfers to all servers on the Name Servers tab
Distribute the zone's trust anchors to the forest's DNS servers
Create a GlobalNames zone that holds the DNSKEY records

explanation: A DNS server can validate DNSSEC responses only if it has a trust anchor for the zone, and AD-integrated signed zones offer an option to distribute trust anchors to all DNS servers in the forest. Stub zones and zone transfers don't create trust anchors, and a GlobalNames zone serves single-label names.

prompt: Windows clients must require DNSSEC validation for names in secure.contoso.com and treat unvalidated responses as failures. How should the administrator configure the clients?

options.text: Add the zone's records to each client's hosts file
Deploy an NRPT rule by Group Policy that requires validation for the namespace
Enable LLMNR so that clients can validate names on the local subnet
Add secure.contoso.com to the clients' DNS suffix search list through Group Policy

explanation: Windows DNS clients are non-validating stub resolvers, and a Name Resolution Policy Table rule tells them to require that their DNS server validated the responses for a namespace. A hosts file bypasses DNS, LLMNR is a link-local fallback without DNSSEC support and the suffix search list only controls how short names are completed.

prompt: A new DHCP server in an AD DS domain has an active scope but doesn't lease any addresses, and its event log says the server isn't authorized. Which command should a domain administrator run?

options.text: Add-DhcpServerInDC -DnsName dhcp2.corp.contoso.com -IPAddress 10.0.0.12
Add-DhcpServerSecurityGroup -ComputerName dhcp2.corp.contoso.com
Set-DhcpServerv4Scope -ScopeId 10.0.1.0 -State Active
Add-DhcpServerv4Failover -ComputerName dhcp2 -PartnerServer dhcp1 -ScopeId 10.0.1.0

explanation: A domain-joined DHCP server must be authorized in Active Directory before it leases addresses, which Add-DhcpServerInDC does. Add-DhcpServerSecurityGroup creates the DHCP Administrators and DHCP Users groups, the scope is already active and a failover relationship doesn't authorize a server.

prompt: Help desk staff must be able to view DHCP scopes, leases and statistics on a server but must not change any configuration. Which group should they be added to?

options.text: DHCP Administrators
DnsUpdateProxy
DHCP Users
Network Configuration Operators

explanation: DHCP Users has read-only access to the DHCP console and its data. DHCP Administrators can change configuration, DnsUpdateProxy lets DHCP servers register DNS records on behalf of clients and Network Configuration Operators can change TCP/IP settings on a computer.

prompt: Clients on a new subnet, 10.30.0.0/24, are separated from the DHCP server by a router. They receive APIPA addresses even though a scope for 10.30.0.0/24 exists on the server. What should be configured?

options.text: A superscope that contains the 10.30.0.0/24 scope and the server's scope
Option 003 Router configured in the 10.30.0.0/24 scope
A DHCP reservation for each client computer on the new subnet
A DHCP relay agent or IP helper on the subnet's router interface

explanation: DHCP discovery relies on broadcasts that routers don't forward, so a relay agent or IP helper on the subnet's router interface must forward the requests to the DHCP server. A superscope groups scopes on one physical segment, option 003 is delivered only after a request reaches the server and reservations also depend on the request arriving.

prompt: Clients receive IP addresses from a scope and can reach hosts on their own subnet but nothing on other subnets. ipconfig shows no default gateway. What should be configured in the scope?

options.text: Option 006 DNS Servers
Option 003 Router
Option 015 DNS Domain Name
Option 044 WINS/NBNS Servers

explanation: Option 003 Router supplies the default gateway that clients need to reach other subnets. Option 006 provides DNS servers, option 015 the DNS domain name and option 044 WINS servers; none of them gives clients a gateway.

prompt: Server-level option 006 lists DNS servers 10.0.0.10 and 10.0.0.11, scope 10.20.0.0/24 sets option 006 to 10.20.0.5 and a reservation in that scope sets option 006 to 10.20.0.9. Which DNS server setting does the reserved client receive?

options.text: All four addresses, merged in order

explanation: The option configured closest to the client wins: reservation options override scope options, which override server options. Values from different levels aren't merged, so the reserved client receives only 10.20.0.9.

prompt: A scope covers 10.10.0.1 to 10.10.0.254. Servers and printers use static addresses from 10.10.0.1 to 10.10.0.20, and DHCP must never lease those addresses. What should be configured?

options.text: A reservation for each address from 10.10.0.1 to 10.10.0.20
A superscope that contains the range 10.10.0.1 to 10.10.0.20
An exclusion range from 10.10.0.1 to 10.10.0.20 in the scope
A shorter lease duration for the scope

explanation: An exclusion range stops the server from leasing addresses in that range while the rest of the scope keeps working. Reservations tie addresses to specific client MAC addresses and are meant to be leased to those clients, a superscope groups whole scopes and lease duration doesn't stop addresses from being leased.

prompt: A single physical network segment has run out of addresses in 192.168.1.0/24. The router interface now also has an address in 192.168.2.0/24, and one DHCP server must lease from both ranges to clients on that segment. What should be created?

options.text: A multicast scope
A split scope
A failover relationship
A superscope that contains both scopes

explanation: A superscope groups several scopes so that one DHCP server can serve multiple logical subnets on the same physical segment. Multicast scopes allocate multicast addresses, a split scope divides one scope between two servers and a failover relationship provides redundancy between two servers.

prompt: A guest Wi-Fi scope fills up during conferences because hundreds of short-lived devices keep their leases for the default eight days. What should the administrator change?

options.text: Increase the lease duration to 30 days
Reduce the scope's lease duration, for example to a few hours
Add an exclusion range that covers half of the scope
Configure option 015 DNS Domain Name in the scope

explanation: A shorter lease duration returns addresses from departed devices to the pool quickly, which suits networks with high turnover. A longer lease makes the shortage worse, an exclusion range removes available addresses and option 015 doesn't affect address availability.

prompt: A network printer with MAC address 00-15-5D-0A-1B-2C must always receive 10.10.0.50 from scope 10.10.0.0. Which command should the administrator run?

options.text: Add-DhcpServerv4Reservation -ScopeId 10.10.0.0 -IPAddress 10.10.0.50 -ClientId 00-15-5D-0A-1B-2C
Add-DhcpServerv4ExclusionRange -ScopeId 10.10.0.0 -StartRange 10.10.0.50 -EndRange 10.10.0.50
Set-DhcpServerv4OptionValue -ScopeId 10.10.0.0 -Router 10.10.0.50
Add-DhcpServerv4Lease -ScopeId 10.10.0.0 -IPAddress 10.10.0.50 -ClientId 00-15-5D-0A-1B-2C -LeaseExpiryTime (Get-Date).AddDays(30)

explanation: Add-DhcpServerv4Reservation binds the address to the client's MAC address (ClientId), so the printer always receives 10.10.0.50. An exclusion prevents anyone from leasing the address, setting the Router option changes the default gateway and a manually created lease expires rather than acting as a permanent reservation.

prompt: A group of IP cameras must always use the same addresses but keep receiving DNS server and gateway changes centrally, without configuring each device. What should be used?

options.text: A static IP configuration on each camera
An exclusion range that covers the cameras' addresses
DHCP reservations for the cameras' MAC addresses
A separate superscope for the cameras

explanation: Reservations give each device a fixed address while it still receives options such as DNS servers and the router from DHCP, so changes are made centrally. Static settings must be changed on every device, an exclusion range only prevents leasing and a superscope groups scopes instead of fixing addresses.

prompt: Each branch office has a local DHCP server. A DHCP server at the head office must take over a branch's scope only if the branch server fails, and the branch server should normally serve all clients. Which configuration should be used?

options.text: DHCP failover in load balance mode with a 50:50 split
DHCP failover in hot standby mode, with the branch server active
A DHCP role on a two-node failover cluster in each branch
A split scope with 80 percent of the addresses on the branch server

explanation: Hot standby mode keeps one server active and the partner on standby, ready to take over if the active server fails, which suits a branch server backed by a central server. Load balance mode shares the client load all the time. A failover cluster needs extra branch hardware and shared storage, and a split scope is an older approach that doesn't replicate lease information.

prompt: An administrator is planning DHCP high availability on Windows Server. Which two statements about DHCP failover are true?

options.text: A failover relationship includes at most two DHCP servers
DHCP failover supports IPv4 scopes only
DHCP failover requires the servers to be nodes of a failover cluster
A scope can have up to four failover partner servers
DHCP failover requires shared storage for the lease database

explanation: A DHCP failover relationship is between two servers and applies to IPv4 scopes, with lease information replicated between the partners. It doesn't use failover clustering or shared storage, and a scope can't have more than one failover partner.

prompt: Two DHCP servers, DHCP1 and DHCP2, must share the 10.10.0.0 scope equally in load balance mode. Which command should be run on DHCP1?

options.text: Add-DhcpServerv4Scope -Name Shared -StartRange 10.10.0.1 -EndRange 10.10.0.254 -SubnetMask 255.255.255.0
Set-DhcpServerv4Scope -ScopeId 10.10.0.0 -State Active
Add-DhcpServerInDC -DnsName DHCP2 -IPAddress 10.10.0.3
Add-DhcpServerv4Failover -Name DHCP1-DHCP2 -PartnerServer DHCP2 -ScopeId 10.10.0.0 -LoadBalancePercent 50

explanation: Add-DhcpServerv4Failover creates the failover relationship with the partner and replicates the scope, and -LoadBalancePercent 50 shares clients equally. Add-DhcpServerv4Scope creates a scope rather than a failover relationship, activating the scope doesn't add a partner and Add-DhcpServerInDC authorizes a server.

prompt: A company needs redundant DHCP service for a stateful DHCPv6 scope by using two Windows DHCP servers. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Split the scope across both servers with non-overlapping ranges
Configure DHCP failover in hot standby mode for the DHCPv6 scope
Configure DHCP failover in load balance mode for the DHCPv6 scope
Create a DHCPv6 superscope that spans both of the servers

explanation: DHCP failover in Windows Server supports only IPv4 scopes, so DHCPv6 redundancy uses a split-scope design with non-overlapping ranges on each server. Neither failover mode applies to DHCPv6, and superscopes are an IPv4 feature on a single server.

prompt: A Windows Server in a branch office shows the IPv4 address 169.254.23.7 after a restart. What does this indicate?

options.text: It received a reserved address from the DHCP server
It has a static IP address that conflicts with another host on the subnet
It couldn't reach a DHCP server and self-assigned an APIPA address
It received an address from an Azure virtual network

explanation: Addresses in 169.254.0.0/16 are Automatic Private IP Addressing addresses that Windows assigns itself when DHCP is enabled but no DHCP server answers. A reservation comes from the scope's range, an address conflict is reported as a duplicate address error and Azure VNets assign addresses from the subnet's range.

prompt: An on-premises network that uses 10.0.0.0/16 is being connected to a new Azure virtual network through a site-to-site VPN. The VNet was created with the address space 10.0.0.0/16, and on-premises hosts can't reach Azure VMs. What is the cause?

options.text: The VPN gateway SKU doesn't support IPv4 routing
Azure VMs must use public IP addresses for site-to-site traffic
The VNet needs an Azure DNS Private Resolver before routing works
The VNet address space overlaps the on-premises network range

explanation: Networks connected through VPN or ExpressRoute must not have overlapping address spaces, because each side routes the shared prefix locally; the VNet has to be readdressed. VPN gateways route IPv4, private addresses are used across site-to-site connections and DNS Private Resolver handles name resolution, not routing.

prompt: Remote users try to map an Azure file share over the internet from home, and the connection fails because their ISP blocks outbound TCP port 445. What is a supported way to give them access?

options.text: Configure the Azure file share to accept SMB traffic on TCP port 443 instead
Connect the users through a point-to-site VPN and access the share over it
Enable SMB 1.0 on the users' client computers
Enable large file shares on the storage account to allow alternative ports

explanation: SMB access to Azure Files uses TCP 445, so when an ISP blocks it, users can connect through a point-to-site or site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute, or use Azure File Sync on a local server. Azure Files doesn't let you change its SMB port, SMB 1.0 isn't supported and large file shares raise capacity limits rather than changing ports.

prompt: A company needs an Azure SMB file share with consistently low latency and high IOPS for an application. Which configuration should be used?

options.text: A premium (SSD) file share in a FileStorage storage account
A transaction optimized file share in a general-purpose v2 account
A cool tier file share in a general-purpose v2 storage account
A hot tier file share in a BlobStorage storage account

explanation: Premium file shares use SSD storage and are created in FileStorage storage accounts, giving consistently low latency and high IOPS. Transaction optimized, hot and cool are HDD-based standard tiers in general-purpose v2 accounts, and BlobStorage accounts can't host Azure file shares.

prompt: An administrator wants to be able to recover an Azure file share if someone accidentally deletes the entire share. What should be enabled on the storage account?

options.text: Share snapshots taken on a daily schedule
Blob versioning
Soft delete for file shares
Geo-redundant storage (GRS) replication

explanation: Soft delete for file shares keeps a deleted share recoverable for the configured retention period. Share snapshots are removed when the share is deleted, blob versioning applies only to blobs and GRS replicates the deletion to the secondary region.

prompt: Hybrid users who authenticate with AD DS need to read, write and delete files on an Azure file share but must not be able to change NTFS permissions. Which share-level role should be assigned to their synced group?

options.text: Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor
Storage Account Contributor
Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor

explanation: Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor grants read, write and delete access over SMB. Elevated Contributor also allows modifying ACLs, Share Reader is read-only and Storage Account Contributor manages the storage account resource rather than granting SMB data access.

prompt: An administrator must set Windows ACLs on directories in an Azure file share by using File Explorer while signed in with an AD DS identity. Which share-level role does the administrator's identity need?

options.text: Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor
Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor
Reader and Data Access

explanation: Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor includes permission to modify ACLs on files and directories over SMB. Share Reader and Share Contributor can't change ACLs, and Reader and Data Access supports tools such as Storage Explorer rather than granting share-level SMB permissions.

prompt: A storage account uses on-premises AD DS authentication, but the AD DS domain isn't synchronized to Microsoft Entra ID. Domain users must access the account's file shares, with access controlled by Windows ACLs. How should share-level permissions be configured?

options.text: Set a default share-level permission for all authenticated identities
Assign RBAC roles to each user's Microsoft Entra identity
Save the storage account access key in each user's Credential Manager
Enable anonymous public access on the storage account

explanation: A default share-level permission applies to every identity that authenticates against the associated AD DS, so users don't need Microsoft Entra identities, and Windows ACLs then control access. RBAC assignments require users or groups synced to Microsoft Entra ID. Distributing the account key bypasses identity-based access, and anonymous access isn't available for Azure file shares.

prompt: Users have hybrid identities synced from AD DS to Microsoft Entra ID. Their Microsoft Entra joined laptops have no network line of sight to domain controllers, but they must access Azure file shares with their identities. Which identity source should be enabled on the storage account?

options.text: On-premises AD DS authentication
Microsoft Entra Domain Services authentication
Microsoft Entra Kerberos
Storage account key authentication

explanation: With Microsoft Entra Kerberos, Microsoft Entra ID issues the Kerberos tickets for Azure Files, so clients don't need to reach domain controllers. On-premises AD DS authentication requires clients to contact a DC, Microsoft Entra Domain Services requires clients joined to that managed domain and account keys don't use user identities.

prompt: An administrator is enabling on-premises AD DS authentication for an Azure Files storage account. Which step registers the storage account in AD DS?

options.text: Run Connect-AzAccount and then New-AzStorageAccountKey
Create a gMSA for the storage account with New-ADServiceAccount
Run Add-Computer -DomainName for the storage account's endpoint
Run Join-AzStorageAccount from the AzFilesHybrid module

explanation: Join-AzStorageAccount, from the AzFilesHybrid module, creates an identity that represents the storage account in AD DS, either a computer account or a service logon account, and enables the AD DS identity source. New-AzStorageAccountKey regenerates keys, gMSAs are used by Windows services rather than storage accounts and Add-Computer joins a Windows machine, not an Azure service.

prompt: An administrator is designing an Azure File Sync deployment. Which statement about sync groups is correct?

options.text: A sync group can contain several cloud endpoints, one per region
A sync group contains one cloud endpoint and one or more server endpoints
A registered server can have only one server endpoint across all sync groups
A sync group must be in the same resource group as the registered servers

explanation: Each sync group has exactly one cloud endpoint, an Azure file share, and can have multiple server endpoints on different registered servers. A registered server can host server endpoints for several sync groups, though not two in the same sync group. Registered servers aren't placed in resource groups; they register with a Storage Sync Service.

prompt: A file server is registered with the Storage Sync Service SSS-East. The administrator wants to add a server endpoint on the same server to a sync group in a different Storage Sync Service, SSS-West. What is the result?

options.text: It can't be done, because a server registers with only one Storage Sync Service
It works, because a server can register with up to three Storage Sync Services
It works only if both Storage Sync Services are in the same Azure region
It works only if cloud tiering is turned off on the server's volumes

explanation: A server can be registered with only one Storage Sync Service at a time, so it can sync only with sync groups in that service. There's no option for multiple registrations, and neither the region nor cloud tiering changes this rule.

prompt: A branch file server with Azure File Sync has a 2 TB data volume. At least 400 GB of the volume must stay free, with the least-used files tiered to Azure first. Which setting should be configured?

options.text: A cloud tiering date policy of 20 days
An Azure file share quota of 1.6 TB
A cloud tiering volume free space policy of 20 percent
Data Deduplication on the volume with the Default usage type

explanation: The volume free space policy tiers the coolest files to the Azure file share whenever free space falls below the set percentage, and 20 percent of 2 TB is 400 GB. A date policy tiers files by days since last access regardless of free space. A share quota limits the size of the cloud share, and deduplication saves space without guaranteeing a free space level.

prompt: An administrator plans to disable cloud tiering on a server endpoint and needs every tiered file brought back to the local volume first. Which cmdlet should be run on the server?

options.text: Invoke-AzStorageSyncChangeDetection
Reset-AzStorageSyncServerCertificate
Invoke-AzStorageSyncCompatibilityCheck
Invoke-StorageSyncFileRecall

explanation: Invoke-StorageSyncFileRecall, one of the Azure File Sync agent's server cmdlets, recalls tiered files to the local volume, and recalls it initiates are persisted to disk. Invoke-AzStorageSyncChangeDetection makes the service detect changes made directly in the Azure file share, Reset-AzStorageSyncServerCertificate rolls the server's certificate and Invoke-AzStorageSyncCompatibilityCheck checks a server for unsupported files and settings.

prompt: On an Azure File Sync server, an administrator wants to confirm that sync sessions are completing and see how many items failed to sync. Where should the administrator look?

options.text: Event ID 4104 in the Windows PowerShell operational log
Event ID 9102 in the FileSync Agent Telemetry event log
Event ID 6008 in the System event log on the registered server
Event ID 4202 in the DFS Replication event log

explanation: Event ID 9102 is written to the Telemetry log under Applications and Services\Microsoft\FileSync\Agent when a sync session completes, and it includes the per-item error count. Event 4104 records PowerShell script blocks, 6008 records an unexpected shutdown and 4202 is a DFS Replication staging warning.

prompt: The storage team wants an email whenever any server endpoint in an Azure File Sync deployment has files that aren't syncing. What should the administrator configure?

options.text: An Azure Monitor metric alert on Files not syncing with an email action group
A Performance Monitor alert on each server for the % Processor Time counter
A data collection rule that collects Security events from the servers
Azure Update Manager periodic assessment for the registered servers

explanation: Azure File Sync publishes metrics such as Files not syncing, Sync session result and Server online status to Azure Monitor, where a metric alert rule can notify an action group. CPU counters, Security event collection and update assessment don't report sync errors.

prompt: A company uses DFS Replication to keep a shared folder synchronized across five branch file servers and wants to replace it with Azure File Sync. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Keep DFS-R running and add Azure File Sync server endpoints on the same replicated folders
Add the Azure file share to the DFS-R replication group as a new member
Add each server's folder as a server endpoint in one sync group, then retire DFS-R
Create a separate sync group and Azure file share for each branch server

explanation: Azure File Sync can replace DFS-R by making the Azure file share the hub of one sync group, with each branch folder added as a server endpoint, after which DFS-R is removed. Running both on the same data isn't supported except in limited cases, such as read-only replicated folders. DFS-R can't replicate to an Azure file share, and separate sync groups would stop the branches from sharing data.

prompt: A company must migrate 300 TB of file share data to Azure Files, and its internet link would need months to transfer it. What should the administrator use for the bulk copy?

options.text: Robocopy over the existing internet link
Storage Migration Service to an Azure VM
Azure File Sync with cloud tiering enabled from the start
Azure Data Box

explanation: Azure Data Box ships physical devices for offline transfer of large data sets into Azure Files when bandwidth is insufficient. Robocopy and Azure File Sync both send the data over the slow link, and Storage Migration Service migrates servers to other Windows Servers rather than seeding Azure Files offline.

prompt: A shared folder grants Everyone Full Control at the share level. The folder's NTFS permissions give the Sales group Read & execute. What access do members of Sales have when they connect over the network?

options.text: Full Control
Read & execute
Modify
No access

explanation: For network access, the more restrictive of the share and NTFS permissions applies, so Sales members get Read & execute. Full Control and Modify exceed the NTFS permission, and Sales does have access because both permission sets grant at least read.

prompt: Users browsing a department share can see the names of folders they can't open, which reveals confidential project names. What should the administrator enable on the share?

options.text: SMB encryption
Continuous availability
Access-based enumeration
Offline files caching set to No files

explanation: Access-based enumeration hides files and folders from users who don't have at least read access to them. SMB encryption protects data in transit, continuous availability supports transparent failover on clustered shares and the offline files setting controls client caching.

prompt: Each user's home folder on a file server must be limited to 10 GB, and users must be prevented from saving files once they reach the limit. What should be configured in File Server Resource Manager?

options.text: A soft quota of 10 GB on each home folder
A passive file screen on the home folders
A file management task that deletes files larger than 10 GB
A hard quota of 10 GB on each home folder

explanation: A hard quota blocks writes that would exceed the limit, while a soft quota only sends notifications and supports reporting. File screens control file types rather than space, and file management tasks expire or act on files rather than enforcing a space limit.

prompt: Users must be prevented from saving video files such as .mp4 and .mkv to a departmental share, and administrators want an email each time someone tries. What should be configured in FSRM?

options.text: An active file screen that uses a video file group, with an email notification
A passive file screen that uses a video file group, with an email notification
A hard quota on the share with an email notification threshold
A classification rule that tags video files as confidential

explanation: An active file screen blocks saving files that match its file groups and can send notifications. A passive file screen only monitors and notifies, a quota limits space rather than file types and classification tags files without blocking them.

prompt: A new home folder is created under D:\Home for each new employee. Each new folder must automatically get a 5 GB quota without an administrator applying it. What should be configured?

options.text: A 5 GB hard quota on the D:\Home folder itself
A weekly Quota Usage storage report scheduled for D:\Home
An auto apply quota on D:\Home with a 5 GB template
A file screen exception on D:\Home

explanation: An auto apply quota on a parent folder applies its quota template to every existing and new subfolder. A quota on D:\Home itself limits the combined size of all home folders, storage reports only report usage and a file screen exception allows file types that would otherwise be blocked.

prompt: Files in a project share that haven't been modified for two years must be moved automatically to an archive folder. What should the administrator configure in FSRM?

options.text: A soft quota on the project share
A file management task that expires files by last modified date
A passive file screen for older file types
A scheduled storage report that lists least recently accessed files

explanation: A file management task runs on a schedule and can expire files that meet a condition, such as not being modified for two years, by moving them to an expiration folder. Quotas and file screens don't move files, and storage reports only list them.

prompt: An administrator is creating a new domain-based DFS namespace and wants access-based enumeration and support for more than 5,000 folders. Which namespace mode should be chosen?

options.text: Stand-alone namespace
Domain-based namespace in Windows 2000 Server mode
Stand-alone namespace hosted on a failover cluster
Domain-based namespace in Windows Server 2008 mode

explanation: Domain-based namespaces in Windows Server 2008 mode support access-based enumeration and scale beyond 5,000 folders. Windows 2000 Server mode lacks those capabilities, and stand-alone namespaces, clustered or not, don't meet the requirement for a domain-based namespace stored in AD DS.

prompt: Branch office servers receive corporate templates through DFS Replication. Changes made at the branches must never replicate back to the head office. What should be configured?

options.text: Make the replicated folder read-only on the branch members
Set the staging quota on the branch members to the minimum value
Disable the connections from the head office to the branches
Configure the branch servers as the primary members

explanation: A read-only replicated folder prevents local changes on those members, so nothing replicates back from the branches. The staging quota affects performance, not direction, disabling connections from the head office stops the branches from receiving updates and primary members win conflicts during initial replication.

prompt: DFS Replication of a folder that holds many large CAD files is slow, and the DFS Replication event log on a member repeatedly shows event ID 4202. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Enable Remote Differential Compression on the connection
Change the replication schedule to replicate only at night
Increase the staging folder quota for the replicated folder
Enable access-based enumeration on the replicated folder

explanation: Event 4202 reports that the staging folder reached its high watermark, so DFS-R repeatedly cleans it up; increasing the staging quota, ideally to at least the size of the largest files being replicated, fixes this. Remote Differential Compression is enabled by default and reduces bandwidth, a night-only schedule slows replication further and access-based enumeration affects visibility, not replication.

prompt: Mobile users must access a file server over the internet with SMB over QUIC instead of a VPN. The file server runs Windows Server 2025 Standard. Which statement is true?

options.text: SMB over QUIC requires Windows Server Datacenter: Azure Edition
SMB over QUIC requires the Datacenter edition of Windows Server 2025
SMB over QUIC requires clients that have SMB 1.0 enabled
SMB over QUIC is supported on Windows Server 2025 Standard

explanation: Starting with Windows Server 2025, the SMB over QUIC server feature is available in Standard and Datacenter editions; previously it required Windows Server 2022 Datacenter: Azure Edition. Datacenter isn't required, and SMB 1.0 is unrelated and insecure; clients use Windows 11.

prompt: An administrator is configuring the perimeter firewall for an SMB over QUIC file server that uses the default port. Which inbound traffic should be allowed?

options.text: TCP 445
UDP 443
TCP 5445
UDP 137 and 138

explanation: SMB over QUIC uses UDP 443 by default, and Microsoft advises against allowing TCP 445 inbound to the file server. TCP 5445 is the default port for SMB over RDMA, and UDP 137 and 138 are legacy NetBIOS ports.

prompt: A certificate with the file server's external FQDN in its subject alternative name is installed in the computer's Personal store. Which cmdlet enables SMB over QUIC with this certificate on a Windows Server 2025 file server?

options.text: New-SmbServerCertificateMapping
Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EncryptData $true
New-SmbShare -EncryptData $true
Set-SmbClientConfiguration -EnableSMBQUIC $true

explanation: New-SmbServerCertificateMapping maps the certificate's thumbprint to the server name and enables SMB over QUIC, and PowerShell is the supported method on Windows Server 2025. The EncryptData settings control SMB encryption, and Set-SmbClientConfiguration changes client behavior rather than the server.

prompt: Users connecting to an SMB over QUIC file server from the internet can't reach domain controllers, so authentication falls back to NTLMv2. The administrator wants them to use Kerberos instead. What should be configured?

options.text: A read-only domain controller with a public IP address
Required SMB signing on all clients
The KDC Proxy service on the file server, used by the clients
